answer:
# Inspection Authorization (IA) and Major Alterations — Regulatory Answer

**Source of record:** eCFR, Title 14. Eligibility: 14 CFR 65.91(c). Privilege/conditions: 14 CFR 65.95(a)(1). Alteration classification: 14 CFR part 43 and Appendix A, with the definition in 14 CFR 1.1. Text below marked **[VERIFIED]** is quoted from the fetched eCFR/ FAA pages (fetch date 2026-11-14). Text marked **[VERIFY]** is cited by section only and must be confirmed against the current eCFR before reliance — I am not asserting its paragraph letter or exact wording here.

---

## 1. Bottom line (the answer in six sentences)

1. "Inspection authorization" is **not a separate certificate** — it is an authorization added to a mechanic certificate, and it is governed by **14 CFR part 65, subpart D** (§§ 65.91, 65.92, 65.93, 65.95).
2. To be **eligible** you must meet five criteria in **§ 65.91(c)**: a currently effective mechanic certificate with **both** airframe and powerplant ratings, each effective and in effect for a total of **at least 3 years**; **at least 2 years** of active engagement immediately before application in maintaining aircraft certificated and maintained under the chapter; a **fixed base of operations** where you can be reached in person or by telephone during a normal working week; **equipment, facilities, and inspection data** available to properly inspect airframes, powerplants, propellers, or related parts/appliances; and a **written test** on inspecting to safety standards for returning aircraft to service **after major repairs and major alterations** and for annual and progressive inspections under part 43.
3. The **privilege** for major alterations is in **§ 65.95(a)(1)**: the IA may **inspect and approve for return to service** an aircraft or related part or appliance after a **major repair or major alteration**, **if the work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator**.
4. That privilege **excludes** aircraft maintained under a **continuous airworthiness program under part 121**.
5. The IA **does not approve the alteration data** — the data must already be FAA-approved (type certificate, STC, PMA, or FAA field approval). The IA approves the *article* for return to service after verifying the work conforms to that approved data. Confusing these two acts is the single most common compliance error in this area.
6. The privilege is exercisable **only while the underlying mechanic certificate (both ratings) and the IA itself remain effective** — see §§ 65.92/65.93 **[VERIFY]**.

---

## 2. Scope note — "qualifications" has two distinct meanings

The word *qualifications* in part 65, subpart D is used for **issuance eligibility** (§ 65.91(c)). The **scope of what an IA may approve regarding major alterations** is stated separately in the **privileges and limitations** rule (§ 65.95). Because the request's phrasing ("qualifications … regarding major alterations") supports both readings, both are answered below. A complete answer needs both, plus (i) the major/minor classification rule and (ii) the record/return-to-service rules, because a valid IA signature is worthless — and unlawful — if applied to an item that is not a major alteration, or applied without the required record entries.

---

## 3. Eligibility to obtain an IA — 14 CFR 65.91(c) **[VERIFIED]**

Verbatim:

> "(c) To be eligible for an inspection authorization, an applicant must—
> (1) Hold a currently effective mechanic certificate with both an airframe rating and a powerplant rating, each of which is currently effective and has been in effect for a total of at least 3 years;
> (2) Have been actively engaged, for at least the 2-year period before the date he applies, in maintaining aircraft certificated and maintained in accordance with this chapter;
> (3) Have a fixed base of operations at which he may be located in person or by telephone during a normal working week but it need not be the place where he will exercise his inspection authority;
> (4) Have available to him the equipment, facilities, and inspection data necessary to properly inspect airframes, powerplants, propellers, or any related part or appliance; and
> (5) Pass a written test on his ability to inspect according to safety standards for returning aircraft to service after major repairs and major alterations and annual and progressive inspections performed under part 43 of this chapter."
> — 14 CFR 65.91(c), https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-65/subpart-D/section-65.91

Element-by-element, with what an auditor would look for:

| # | Criterion | Threshold / test | Evidence a reviewer expects |
|---|---|---|---|
| (c)(1) | Mechanic certificate with **both** A and P ratings | Each rating currently effective **and** in effect a total of **at least 3 years** | Certificate number and issue dates; both ratings shown |
| (c)(2) | Actively engaged in maintaining aircraft certificated/maintained under 14 CFR chapter I | **At least the 2-year period immediately before application** | Employment/work history, employer letters, logbooks, work orders |
| (c)(3) | Fixed base of operations | Reachable in person or by telephone during a normal working week; need not be where authority is exercised | Address/phone on application; changes reported |
| (c)(4) | Equipment, facilities, and inspection data available | Sufficient to properly inspect airframes, powerplants, propellers, or related parts/appliances | Tool list, facility description, current technical data library |
| (c)(5) | Written test | Must pass; content is inspection to safety standards for **return to service after major repairs and major alterations** and for annual/progressive inspections under part 43 | IA knowledge test results |

**Note the direct link to the question:** § 65.91(c)(5) is the qualification that *is specifically about major alterations*. The IA knowledge test exists in substantial part to establish that the holder can determine whether a major repair or major alteration conforms to approved data and is safe to return to service. That is the competency the privilege in § 65.95(a)(1) then authorizes the holder to exercise.

Application mechanics (§ 65.91(a)–(b)) — form and manner prescribed by the Administrator; an applicant meeting the section is entitled to the authorization. **[VERIFY]** paragraph content beyond (c).

---

## 4. The major-alteration privilege and its conditions — 14 CFR 65.95(a) **[VERIFIED]**

Verbatim:

> "(a) The holder of an inspection authorization may—
> (1) Inspect and approve for return to service any aircraft or related part or appliance (except any aircraft maintained in accordance with a continuous airworthiness program under part 121 of this chapter) after a major repair or major alteration to it in accordance with part 43 [New] of this chapter, if the work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator; and
> (2) Perform an annual, or perform or supervise a progressive inspection according to §§ 43.13 and 43.15 of this chapter."
> — 14 CFR 65.95(a), https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-65/subpart-D/section-65.95

("[New]" is an editorial artifact in the published text, not substantive.)

Decomposed into the six elements an IA must be able to satisfy on demand:

| Element | Regulatory words | What it means operationally |
|---|---|---|
| **Who** | "The holder of an inspection authorization" | A currently effective IA on a currently effective mechanic certificate with both ratings. An expired IA, or a lapsed A or P rating, removes the privilege entirely. |
| **What** | "any aircraft or related part or appliance" | Aircraft, airframe, engine, propeller, appliance, or component — not limited to the whole aircraft. |
| **When** | "after a major repair or major alteration to it" | The classification gate. If the work is **minor**, § 65.95(a)(1) is not the operative authority (see § 6). |
| **Exclusion** | "except any aircraft maintained in accordance with a continuous airworthiness program under part 121" | Part 121 continuous-airworthiness aircraft are outside the IA's § 65.95(a)(1) approval authority; approval flows through the operator's approved program. |
| **Precondition** | "if the work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator" | The data must already be FAA-approved. **The IA approves the work/article, not the data.** No approved data → no lawful approval, regardless of workmanship quality. |
| **Act** | "inspect and approve for return to service" | A personal, two-part act: an actual inspection, then a return-to-service approval. FAA guidance states the holder must **personally** perform the inspection and determine that the repair or alteration data has FAA approval. |

### 4.1 The critical distinction (compliance core)

- **Data approval** = an FAA function (type design, STC, PMA, or field approval by an authorized FAA representative). An IA cannot create, extend, or waive approved data.
- **Return-to-service approval** = the IA function under § 65.95(a)(1), conditioned on the work having been done *in accordance with* already-approved data.
- If approved data does not exist, the correct action is **do not approve**; the data-approval path (e.g., FAA field approval or STC) must be pursued first. Signing off and hoping the data is acceptable converts an administrative gap into an airworthiness violation under part 91.

### 4.2 Currency gates on exercising the privilege **[VERIFY]**

Sections 65.92 (duration) and 65.93 (renewal) were **not** captured in the verified passages. They are cited at section level only; confirm paragraph text at the eCFR before relying:

- **Duration/expiry:** the IA expires on a fixed biennial date (odd-numbered years), and the holder may exercise the privileges only while holding a currently effective mechanic certificate with both ratings currently effective. **[VERIFY — 14 CFR 65.92]**
- **Ceases to be effective:** the authorization ceases to be effective if the holder loses the fixed base of operations, loses the required equipment/facilities/inspection data, or is no longer actively engaged in maintaining aircraft under the chapter. **[VERIFY — 14 CFR 65.93]**
- **Renewal:** renewal is activity/currency based (recent inspection and major repair/alteration experience, refresher training, or testing, within the preceding 24-month window, per the current rule and the FAA IA Information Guide). **The exact activity counts and training hours must be read from the current § 65.93 and the current guide — do not rely on secondhand summaries.** **[VERIFY]**

---

## 5. Is it actually a "major alteration"? — classification gate

This determination comes **before** § 65.95(a)(1) can be applied.

| Step | Authority | Content |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **14 CFR 1.1** (definition) | A major alteration is an alteration not listed in the aircraft, aircraft engine, or propeller specifications that (1) might appreciably affect weight, balance, structural strength, performance, powerplant operation, flight characteristics, or other qualities affecting airworthiness; or (2) is not done according to accepted practices or cannot be done by elementary operations. **[VERIFY exact wording]** |
| 2 | **14 CFR part 43, Appendix A** | Enumerated major alterations by category — airframe, powerplant, propeller, appliance. If the alteration appears in the list, it is major regardless of the general test. **[VERIFY list]** |
| 3 | **14 CFR 43.3 / 43.7** | Who may perform the work and who may approve it for return to service. A **minor** alteration is not routed through § 65.95(a)(1). **[VERIFY]** |

**Rule of construction:** Appendix A is a floor, not a ceiling. An alteration not listed can still be major under the § 1.1 appreciable-effect test. When classification is genuinely ambiguous, treat it as major and obtain data approval — the downside of over-classifying is administrative; the downside of under-classifying is an unairworthy aircraft in service.

---

## 6. Records and return-to-service paperwork that complete the act

An IA approval that is not properly recorded is an incomplete approval.

| Item | Authority | Requirement |
|---|---|---|
| Return-to-service statement | **14 CFR 43.5** **[VERIFY]** | Approval must be recorded with the required statement, signature, certificate number, and kind of certificate. |
| Maintenance record entry | **14 CFR 43.9** **[VERIFY]** | Description of work, date, and the approving person's signature/certificate number. |
| **FAA Form 337** | **14 CFR 43.9** (major repair/alteration record provision) **[VERIFY paragraph letter]** | Major repairs and major alterations require Form 337, with the **approved data cited** (STC number, field approval, etc.) and disposition copy to the FAA. This is where the "approved technical data" precondition becomes auditable. |
| Owner/operator records | **14 CFR 91.417** **[VERIFY]** | Records retained and made available. |
| Airworthiness responsibility | **14 CFR 91.403(a)** **[VERIFY]** | The owner/operator remains primarily responsible for airworthiness; the IA's approval does not transfer that responsibility. |

---

## 7. Practical decision procedure (apply in order)

1. **Is my IA effective today, and is my mechanic certificate effective with both A and P ratings?** If no → stop; no privilege exists.
2. **Is the article an aircraft maintained under a part 121 continuous airworthiness program?** If yes → § 65.95(a)(1) does not authorize the approval; route through the operator's program.
3. **Is the work a major alteration** (Appendix A list, or the § 1.1 appreciable-effect test)? If it is minor → § 65.95(a)(1) is not the authority; approve under the applicable mechanic/return-to-service rule.
4. **Does FAA-approved technical data exist for this alteration** (TC, STC, PMA, or field approval)? If no → do not approve; the data-approval path must be completed first.
5. **Did I personally inspect the work and find it conforms to that approved data?** If no → do not approve.
6. **Record it:** return-to-service statement (§ 43.5), maintenance entry (§ 43.9), Form 337 for the major alteration with the approved data cited, and the required distribution.

---

## 8. Compliance pitfalls (what actually gets violated)

| # | Pitfall | Why it fails | Correct action |
|---|---|---|---|
| P1 | Treating the IA signature as *approval of the alteration/design* | § 65.95(a)(1) conditions the approval on data **already** approved by the Administrator | Cite the actual approved data on Form 337; if none exists, obtain data approval first |
| P2 | Approving a major alteration on a part 121 continuous-airworthiness aircraft | Express exclusion in § 65.95(a)(1) | Route through the operator's approved program |
| P3 | Exercising the privilege on a lapsed IA or lapsed A/P rating | §§ 65.92/65.93 currency gates **[VERIFY]** | Verify currency before every approval |
| P4 | Assuming "acceptable methods" guidance equals "approved data" | The regulation requires data **approved by the Administrator**; whether a specific acceptable-methods procedure qualifies is a data-approval question for the FAA, not a judgment call for the IA | Do not assume; confirm the data's approval status with the FAA before approving |
| P5 | Misclassifying a major alteration as minor to avoid the data/Form 337 burden | Appendix A plus the § 1.1 appreciable-effect test; under-classification puts an unairworthy article in service | Classify conservatively; document the basis |
| P6 | Approving without a personal inspection | § 65.95(a)(1) requires the holder to inspect; FAA guidance requires the holder to personally perform the inspection | Inspect personally; do not delegate the approval decision |
| P7 | Independence/self-approval — approving work the IA personally performed | Whether this is permitted depends on the current text of the return-to-service rules and FAA guidance; **not confirmed from the sources gathered** | Treat as an open item (§ 9) and confirm before relying on it |

---

## 9. Verification log and open items

**Verified verbatim (safe to quote):**
- 14 CFR 65.91(c)(1)–(5) — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-65/subpart-D/section-65.91
- 14 CFR 65.95(a)(1)–(2) — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-65/subpart-D/section-65.95
- FAA *Inspection Authorization Information Guide* — states the basic functions of the IA holder are set forth in § 65.95, and that an IA may inspect and approve for return to service after a major repair or major alteration (with the part 121 exception) — https://www.faa.gov/sites/faa.gov/files/2022-07/ia_info_guide.pdf

**Cited by section only — confirm before relying:** §§ 65.91(a)–(b); 65.92; 65.93; 43.3; 43.5; 43.7; 43.9; 43.13; 43.15; part 43 Appendix A; 1.1; 91.403; 91.417.

**Open items (outside what the gathered sources establish):**
1. The **specific FAA order or advisory circular governing field approval** of major repairs/alterations (the research flagged the order number as unverified — do not cite a number until confirmed).
2. **IA renewal activity counts and training hours** — read from the current § 65.93 and current IA Information Guide.
3. **Self-approval independence** (P7) — confirm against § 43.7 and current FAA guidance.
4. **Repair station / part 145 and air carrier paths** for approving major alterations — parallel approval routes that are not part of the IA privilege and were not verified here.

**Currency caution:** eCFR text was fetched 2026-11-14. Regulations change; re-pull the four cited sections at the eCFR before using this as a compliance basis, and use the eCFR's point-in-time feature if the approval date matters.

---

## 10. One-paragraph answer for a study/exam context

Under 14 CFR part 65, subpart D, an Inspection Authorization is held by a mechanic who has held a currently effective mechanic certificate with **both** airframe and powerplant ratings for a total of at least **3 years**, has been actively engaged for at least the **2 years** before applying in maintaining aircraft certificated and maintained under the chapter, has a **fixed base of operations** where he can be reached during a normal working week, has the **equipment, facilities, and inspection data** necessary to properly inspect airframes, powerplants, propellers, and related parts or appliances, and has **passed a written test** on inspecting to safety standards for returning aircraft to service **after major repairs and major alterations** and for annual and progressive inspections under part 43. Having the authorization, the holder may **inspect and approve for return to service** an aircraft or related part or appliance after a **major repair or major alteration** — **except** aircraft maintained under a **part 121 continuous airworthiness program** — **only if the work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator**. The IA inspects and approves the *work*, not the *data*.

question: IA
answer:
# Inspection Authorization (IA) — Qualifications and Authority for Major Alterations
## Governing law: 14 CFR Part 65, Subpart D, read with 14 CFR Part 43

---

## 1. Direct answer

The **qualifications** for an Inspection Authorization are set out in **14 CFR § 65.91(c)(1)–(5)**. There are five, and all five must be met.

The **authority to inspect and approve a major alteration for return to service** is in **14 CFR § 65.95(a)(1)**, and it carries two conditions on its face: the work must have been done **in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator**, and the aircraft must **not** be one maintained under a **Part 121 continuous airworthiness program**.

What counts as a **major alteration** is defined in **Appendix A to Part 43**; the approval and record mechanics around it are in **§§ 43.3, 43.5, 43.7, 43.9** and **Appendix B to Part 43** (FAA Form 337).

---

## 2. The five qualification requirements — § 65.91(c)

Quoted verbatim from eCFR (fetched 2026-11-14, sha256 8dd2b52b76db):

> **(c) To be eligible for an inspection authorization, an applicant must—**
>
> **(1)** Hold a currently effective mechanic certificate with both an airframe rating and a powerplant rating, each of which is currently effective and has been in effect for a total of at least **3 years**;
>
> **(2)** Have been actively engaged, for at least the **2-year** period before the date he applies, in maintaining aircraft certificated and maintained in accordance with this chapter;
>
> **(3)** Have a **fixed base of operations** at which he may be located in person or by telephone during a normal working week but it need not be the place where he will exercise his inspection authority;
>
> **(4)** Have available to him the **equipment, facilities, and inspection data** necessary to properly inspect airframes, powerplants, propellers, or any related part or appliance; and
>
> **(5)** **Pass a written test** on his ability to inspect according to safety standards for returning aircraft to service after **major repairs and major alterations** and annual and progressive inspections performed under part 43 of this chapter.

### What each one means in practice

| # | Cite | Requirement | Practitioner reading |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | § 65.91(c)(1) | Mechanic certificate, Airframe **and** Powerplant, each currently effective, in effect a total of at least 3 years | You must already be a rated A&P. The 3-year clock runs on the **ratings**, and both ratings are required — an airframe-only or powerplant-only mechanic is not eligible. |
| 2 | § 65.91(c)(2) | Actively engaged for the 2-year period before application in maintaining aircraft certificated/maintained under the chapter | The 2 years is measured immediately before application and must be actual engagement in this chapter's aircraft, not general mechanical work. |
| 3 | § 65.91(c)(3) | Fixed base of operations, reachable in person or by telephone during a normal working week | The base need not be where the IA exercises authority. It is a contactability requirement, not a shop requirement. |
| 4 | § 65.91(c)(4) | Equipment, facilities, and inspection data available | You must actually hold the technical data and tooling to inspect what you sign for. This is the hook the FAA uses when an IA signs work beyond his data. |
| 5 | § 65.91(c)(5) | Pass the written test | The test is expressly scoped to **return to service after major repairs and major alterations** and to annual/progressive inspections. Major alterations are therefore a named subject of the IA test itself. |

Supporting procedural paragraphs (paraphrase — verify wording against eCFR before quoting): § 65.91(a) requires application on a form and in a manner prescribed by the Administrator; § 65.91(b) provides that an applicant who meets the requirements of the section is entitled to the authorization.

**FAA-AMT relevance:** the IA is a **separate certificate** from the mechanic certificate. Passing the A&P tests does not confer it; § 65.91(c)(5) is a distinct written test, and the FAA publishes a separate IA information guide (faa.gov/sites/faa.gov/files/ia_info_guide.pdf). The Aviation Mechanic ACS covers A&P airman certification, not IA — IA content is governed by § 65.91(c)(5) and the FAA's IA testing program.

---

## 3. The privilege that actually touches major alterations — § 65.95(a)

Quoted verbatim from eCFR (fetched 2026-11-14, sha256 04eedc455339):

> **(a) The holder of an inspection authorization may—**
>
> **(1)** Inspect and approve for return to service any aircraft or related part or appliance **(except any aircraft maintained in accordance with a continuous airworthiness program under part 121 of this chapter)** after a major repair or major alteration to it in accordance with part 43 of this chapter, **if the work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator**; and
>
> **(2)** Perform an annual, or perform or supervise a progressive inspection according to §§ 43.13 and 43.15 of this chapter.

### The three conditions embedded in (a)(1)

1. **Subject matter** — the article is an aircraft or a related part or appliance. (Not instruments or propellers as a general mechanic privilege under § 65.81; the IA privilege in § 65.95(a)(1) is written on the aircraft/part/appliance.)
2. **Part 121 carve-out** — the IA may **not** use this authority on an aircraft maintained under a Part 121 continuous airworthiness program. For those aircraft, approval runs through the certificate holder's own authority (§ 121.379) under its approved program, not through an IA.
3. **Approved data condition** — the work must have been done **in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator**. This is the operational heart of the answer:
   - If the alteration is covered by an **STC, an approved model list (AML), or other Administrator-approved data**, the IA can inspect and approve for return to service.
   - If there is **no Administrator-approved data** — the classic non-STC'd alteration — the IA **cannot** approve it. The data must first be approved by the FAA (field approval, or a design approval). The IA's signature does not substitute for data approval.

§ 65.95(b) contains the limitations on exercise of the authority; the operative limit for this question is the same approved-data condition carried in (a)(1). The verbatim enumeration of § 65.95(b) was not captured in this research pass — quote it from eCFR directly before relying on its exact wording.

---

## 4. What counts as a "major alteration" — Appendix A to Part 43

The threshold matters because it changes **who** may approve. Appendix A to Part 43 lists major alterations by category:

- **(a)(1) Airframe major alterations** — alterations of wings, tail surfaces, fuselage, engine mounts, control systems, landing gear, hull, and floats, **when not listed in the aircraft specifications issued by the FAA**.
- **(a)(2) Powerplant major alterations** — e.g., converting an engine from one approved model to another involving changes in compression ratio, propeller reduction gear, or impeller gear ratios, or substitution of major engine parts requiring extensive rework and testing; replacing engine structural parts with parts not supplied by the original manufacturer or not specifically approved by the Administrator; installing an accessory not approved for the engine; removing accessories listed as required equipment; installing structural parts other than the type approved for the installation; conversions to use fuel of a rating or grade other than that listed in the engine specifications.
- **(a)(3) Propeller major alterations.**
- **(a)(4) Appliance major alterations.**

Appendix A also contains the **major repair** list, which is the counterpart used with § 65.95(a)(1).

FAA guidance (not regulation text) applies the general test: an alteration is major if it might appreciably affect weight, balance, structural strength, performance, powerplant operation, flight characteristics, or other qualities affecting airworthiness, or if it cannot be done by elementary operations — see FAA Order 8900.1 Vol. 5 Ch. 5 and **AC 43-210A**, *Standardized Procedures for Requesting Approval of Data for Major Alterations via Field Approval*. Verify current revision status of both before citing them in a compliance document.

---

## 5. The Part 43 approval chain around the IA signature

| Cite | Function |
|---|---|
| **§ 43.3** | Persons authorized to perform maintenance, preventive maintenance, rebuilding, and alterations — mechanic certificate holders (§ 43.3(b)), repairmen (§ 43.3(c)), persons under supervision (§ 43.3(d)), repair stations (§ 43.3(e)), air carriers/operating certificate holders (§ 43.3(f)). This governs **who may do the work**; it does not by itself authorize return to service after a major alteration. |
| **§ 43.5** | Approval for return to service after maintenance, preventive maintenance, rebuilding, or alteration. Requires the maintenance record entry and, where applicable, the repair/alteration form. |
| **§ 43.7** | Persons authorized to approve for return to service. This is the section that pairs with § 65.95(a)(1) for major alterations. |
| **§ 43.9** | Content, form, and disposition of maintenance, preventive maintenance, and alteration records — the description, date, and signature requirement. |
| **Appendix B to Part 43** | Prescribes execution and disposition of the major repair/alteration form (**FAA Form 337**) by the person performing the work, with the required approval for return to service. |
| **§ 65.81** | General mechanic privileges and limitations — a mechanic may perform and supervise maintenance, preventive maintenance, and alterations for which rated, but **excluding major repairs to and major alterations of propellers, and any repair to or alteration of instruments**; also carries the 24-month recent-experience condition. |

**Net rule for the AMT:** an A&P **performs** the major alteration and executes the Form 337 entry; an **IA (or the Administrator, or a Part 145 repair station / Part 121 or 135 certificate holder acting under its own approval authority) approves it for return to service.** An A&P without IA authority cannot return a major alteration to service on his own signature.

---

## 6. Who else can approve a major alteration for return to service

The IA is one route, not the only route. For completeness, since "inspection auth" in the question could be read broadly:

- **The Administrator** — field approval of the alteration data (Form 337 with FAA block signed), or approval via STC/design approval. Governed by § 43.7 and FAA Order 8900.1; procedure in AC 43-210A.
- **Part 145 repair station** — may perform and approve within its ratings and limitations under Part 145 (see § 145.201 privileges and limitations) for work it maintains; it does not approve alteration **data**, and it is not a substitute for an IA on aircraft it does not maintain.
- **Part 121 / Part 135 certificate holder** — approval by its authorized personnel under its manual, per **§ 121.379** (authority to perform and approve maintenance, preventive maintenance, and alterations) and **§ 135.437**. This is why § 65.95(a)(1) carves out Part 121 continuous-airworthiness aircraft.

---

## 7. Renewal and currency — § 65.93

An IA is renewed for a **2-year period**, on or before **March 31 of each odd-numbered year**, with evidence that the holder still meets § 65.91(c)(1)–(4), plus evidence of recent activity or refresher training during the 24 months before expiration (annual inspections at a specified rate, major repairs/alterations at a specified rate, progressive inspections, an acceptable refresher course of not less than 8 hours, or an oral test by an FAA inspector). The exact enumeration and rates in § 65.93 were not captured verbatim in this research pass — **quote § 65.93 from eCFR directly** rather than from this summary.

---

## 8. Common traps worth flagging for AMT study use

1. **IA ≠ mechanic certificate.** Separate application, separate test (§ 65.91(a), (c)(5)).
2. **IA ≠ repair station authorization.** A repair station's internal approval authority is not an IA and does not satisfy § 65.95.
3. **No approved data, no IA approval.** § 65.95(a)(1) is conditional on Administrator-approved technical data. Field approval or an STC must exist first.
4. **Part 121 continuous airworthiness aircraft are excluded** on the face of § 65.95(a)(1).
5. **Performing ≠ approving.** § 43.3 governs who may do the work; § 43.7/§ 65.95 govern who may approve it for return to service.
6. **Both ratings.** § 65.91(c)(1) requires airframe **and** powerplant, each in effect at least 3 years.
7. **Fixed base is a contactability test**, not a shop-location test (§ 65.91(c)(3)).

---

question: IA
answer:
ANSWER — FAA AMT / Inspection Authorization (IA) and major alterations (U.S. 14 CFR, current eCFR)

Short answer: For a major alteration, the person who may inspect and approve the aircraft, airframe, engine, propeller, appliance, or component part for return to service is the holder of an FAA Inspection Authorization (IA), under 14 CFR §65.95(a)(1), if the work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator and the aircraft is not maintained under a Part 121 continuous airworthiness program. An A&P mechanic certificate (the FAA-AMT credential) by itself is not the IA privilege; the mechanic must also hold the IA, or the approval must be made by another person or entity authorized under §43.7 (for example, a Part 145 repair station or a Part 121/135 air carrier within its approved scope).

1. Eligibility to hold the IA — 14 CFR §65.91
- Mechanic certificate: hold a currently effective mechanic certificate with both an airframe rating and a powerplant rating, each currently effective and in effect for a total of at least 3 years — §65.91(c)(1).
- Active experience: have been actively engaged in maintaining aircraft for at least 2 years of the 3-year period preceding the date of application — §65.91(c)(2).
- Fixed base: have a fixed base of operations — §65.91(c)(3).
- Equipment/facilities: have available equipment, facilities, and materials to perform the required inspections — §65.91(c)(4).
- Application: apply on the form and in the manner prescribed by the Administrator — §65.91(a).
- Duration: an IA is effective for 2 years under §65.92 and is renewed under §65.93; renewal/currency is separate from the major-alteration conditions below.

2. The major-alteration privilege and conditions — §65.95(a)(1)
The eCFR text (quoted from the fetched §65.95 page) states:
'The holder of an inspection authorization may— (1) Inspect and approve for return to service any aircraft or related part or appliance (except any aircraft maintained in accordance with a continuous airworthiness program under part 121 of this chapter) after a major repair or major alteration to it in accordance with part 43 of this chapter, if the work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator; and ...'

Conditions that must be met for the IA to use that privilege on a major alteration:
- The item must be a major repair or major alteration. 'Major alteration' is defined in §1.1 and listed in Part 43 Appendix A.
- The work must have been done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator (for example, an STC, an FAA field approval, or other FAA-approved data). If the data is not approved, the IA cannot approve the alteration.
- The work must be in accordance with Part 43.
- The aircraft must not be maintained under a Part 121 continuous airworthiness program. For such aircraft, the Part 121 air carrier's approval path applies, not the IA's §65.95(a)(1) privilege.
- The IA must inspect the configuration for conformity to the approved data and the performance standards of Part 43, then make the return-to-service approval.

3. Limits — §65.95(b)
- The IA may not approve a major repair or major alteration unless the work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator.
- The IA may not approve a major repair or major alteration of a propeller.
- The Part 121 continuous-airworthiness exclusion in §65.95(a)(1) applies.
- Part 135 is not named in the §65.95(a)(1) exception; do not state a categorical Part 135 bar. Check the specific operating rule and the air carrier's manual/program.

4. Records and paperwork
- Maintenance record entry under §43.9.
- A major alteration requires FAA Form 337; the approving IA signs the return-to-service approval block.
- If the alteration changes operating limitations or FAA-approved flight manual data, §43.7(a)(3) requires those limitations/data to be revised as prescribed in §91.9.
- The alteration must be supported by approved data; a field approval is obtained on Form 337 when no other approved data exists.

5. Practical sign-off checklist for an IA
1. Classify the work: major alteration under §1.1 and Part 43 Appendix A.
2. Confirm approved technical data: STC, FAA field approval, or other data approved by the Administrator.
3. Confirm the work was performed by persons authorized under §43.3 and in accordance with Part 43.
4. Inspect the installation for conformity to the approved data and Part 43 performance standards.
5. Complete the §43.9 record entry and FAA Form 337.
6. Confirm no Part 121 continuous-airworthiness conflict and no propeller major repair/alteration limitation.
7. Sign the return-to-service approval only when all conditions are met.

6. Key distinction for an FAA-AMT
An A&P mechanic may perform or supervise maintenance, preventive maintenance, and alterations for which rated under §65.81 and §43.3, but the §65.95(a)(1) approval-after-major-alteration privilege belongs to the IA holder. The practical answer is therefore: A&P plus IA, with the specific major-alteration conditions of §65.95(a)(1), not an A&P certificate alone.
